subject: physics
title: Coulomb's law and electric field strength
key_idea: An electric field is a region where a charge feels a force. Its strength is the force per unit positive charge, E = F/Q. Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges, and from it E = Q/(4πε₀r²) for a point charge.

blocks.text: Electric fields are due to charges. This section defines the field, shows how to draw it and links field strength to force.

items.meaning: A region in which a charged particle experiences a force.
The force per unit positive charge on a small positive test charge.

blocks.label: Electric field strength
where: E = electric field strength (N/C, same as V/m)
Q = the charge in the field (C)

blocks.label: Force on a charge in a field

items: The field is a vector. Its direction is the direction of the force on a positive charge.
A negative charge feels a force in the opposite direction to the field.
Field lines show the direction of the force on a small positive charge.
Lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges, and they never cross.
The closer together the lines, the stronger the field.
Around a point charge the field is **radial**: straight out for positive, straight in for negative.
An electric field is a region where a charge feels a force.
E = F/Q is the force per unit positive charge, so F = QE.
Field lines go from positive to negative; closer lines mean a stronger field.

blocks.text: Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges in a vacuum. Air can be treated as a vacuum for this calculation.

blocks.label: Coulomb's law
where: ε₀ = permittivity of free space (8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m)

items: The force is proportional to the **product of the charges**.
The force is inversely proportional to the **square of the distance**.
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. The two forces are equal and opposite.
For a charged sphere or conductor, the charge can be taken as a point charge at its **centre**, for points outside it.
The constant 1/(4πε₀) is about 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².

items: F = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r²): an inverse-square law.
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
A charged sphere acts as a point charge at its centre.

blocks.text: Put a small test charge q at distance r from a point charge Q. Coulomb's law gives the force, and E = F/q gives the field.

blocks.label: Field strength of a point charge
where: ε₀ = permittivity of free space (8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m)

items: E falls as 1/r²: double the distance and E falls to a quarter.
The direction is away from a positive Q and towards a negative Q.
The test charge q cancels, so E does not depend on it.

diagram.alt: A calculation of the electric field strength at a distance from a point charge, with new numbers each time.
diagram.question: Calculate the electric field strength {r} cm from a point charge of {Q} nC in air. (1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) Give your answer in kN/C.

items: E = Q/(4πε₀r²) for a point charge, or for a sphere outside it.
E points away from positive charge and towards negative charge.
E falls as 1/r².

checks.a: The force per unit positive charge acting on a small positive test charge at that point (E = F/Q).

checks.q: Two point charges exert a force F on each other. State the new force if the charges are kept the same and the distance between them is halved.
checks.a: F is proportional to 1/r². Halving r makes the force four times larger, 4F.

checks.q: Derive E = Q/(4πε₀r²) for the field strength of a point charge Q.
checks.a: The force on a small test charge q at distance r is F = Qq/(4πε₀r²). Field strength is force per unit charge, E = F/q. Dividing and cancelling q gives E = Q/(4πε₀r²).

blocks.text: Compare the gravitational and electrostatic forces between subatomic particles.

items: Both forces follow an inverse-square law, but the electrostatic force between a proton and an electron is about 10³⁹ times larger than the gravitational force.
The electric force depends on charges of about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Gravity depends on masses of about 10⁻²⁷ kg and on the very small constant G.
So gravity is negligible between subatomic particles.
